# `geoWithin` Operator  
## Definition  
The `geoWithin` operator supports querying geographic points within a given geometry. Only points are returned, even if `indexShapes` value is `true` in the [index definition.](/docs/search/index/field-types/geo-type#std-label-bson-data-types-geo)  
You can query points within a:  
- Circle  
- Bounding box  
- Polygon  
When specifying the coordinates to search, longitude must be specified first and then the latitude. Longitude values can be between `-180` and `180`, both inclusive. Latitude values can be between `-90` and `90`, both inclusive. Coordinate values can be integers or doubles.  
**Note:**  
MongoDB Search does not support the following:  
- Non-default coordinate reference system (CRS)  
- Planar XY coordinate system (2 dimensional)  
- Coordinate pairs Point notation (that is, `pointFieldName: [12, 34]`)

## Options  
`geoWithin` uses the following terms to construct a query:  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `box` | object | Object that specifies the bottom left and top right [GeoJSON](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geospatial-indexes-store-geojson) points of a box to search within. The object takes the following fields: `bottomLeft` - Bottom left GeoJSON [point.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geojson-point); `topRight` - Top right GeoJSON [point.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geojson-point) To learn how to specify GeoJSON data inside a GeoJSON object, see [GeoJSON Objects.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geospatial-indexes-store-geojson) Either `box`, `circle`, or `geometry` is required. | conditional |
| `circle` | object | Object that specifies the center point and the radius in meters to search within. The object contains the following [GeoJSON](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geospatial-indexes-store-geojson) fields: `center` - Center of the circle specified as a GeoJSON [point.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geojson-point); `radius` - Radius, which is a number, specified in meters. Value must be greater than or equal to `0`. To learn how to specify GeoJSON data inside a GeoJSON object, see [GeoJSON Objects.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geospatial-indexes-store-geojson) Either `circle`, `box`, or `geometry` is required. | conditional |
| `geometry` | GeoJSON object | [GeoJSON](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geospatial-indexes-store-geojson) object that specifies the [MultiPolygon](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geojson-multipolygon) or [Polygon](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geojson-polygon) to search within. The polygon must be specified as a closed loop where the last position is the same as the first position. When calculating geospatial results, MongoDB Search [geoShape](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/geoShape#std-label-geoshape-ref) and [geoWithin](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/geoWithin#std-label-geowithin-ref) operators and MongoDB [$geoIntersects](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/geoIntersects/) operator use different geometries. This difference can be seen in how MongoDB Search and MongoDB draw polygonal edges. MongoDB Search draws polygons based on [Cartesian distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_coordinate_system), which is the shortest line between two points in the coordinate reference system. MongoDB draws polygons using the geodesic mode based on [2dsphere indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2dsphere/) that is built on top of a third-party library for [geodesic types](https://s2geometry.io/devguide/basic_types), or the flat mode, from [2d indexes](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/indexes/index-types/geospatial/2d/). To learn more, see [GeoJSON Objects.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#polygon) MongoDB Search and MongoDB could return different results for geospatial queries involving polygons. To learn how to specify GeoJSON data inside a GeoJSON object, see [GeoJSON Objects.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geospatial-indexes-store-geojson) Either `geometry`, `box`, or `circle` is required. | conditional |
| `path` | string or array of strings | Indexed [geo](/docs/search/index/field-types/geo-type#std-label-bson-data-types-geo) type field or fields to search. | yes |

| `score` | object | Score to assign to matching search results. By default, the [score](/docs/search/query/score/overview#std-label-scoring-ref) in the results is `1`. You can modify the score using the following options: `boost`: multiply the result score by the given number.; `constant`: replace the result score with the given number.; `function`: replace the result score with the given expression. For information on using `score` in your query, see [Score the Documents in the Results.](/docs/search/query/score/overview#std-label-scoring-ref) | no |

The following query uses the `geoWithin` operator with the `box` field to search for properties within a bounding box in Australia.

# `hasAncestor` Operator  
## Definition  
The `hasAncestor` operator queries an `embeddedDocuments` type field that you specify in the `ancestorPath`. The `ancestorPath` is a parent of the field that you specify in the `returnScope`. The `returnScope` specifies the nested field, including the level of nesting, that you want to retrieve.  
You can use this operator when scoring and retrieving objects within arrays as independent documents to:  
- Filter on ancestor fields (higher level of nesting).  
- Filter on sibling fields (equal level of nesting).

## Fields  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ancestorPath` | String | Name of the `embeddedDocuments` type field that is an intermediary ancestor of the nested field used in the query. This is the parent document that the operator evaluates. | Required |
| `operator` | Object | Operator to use to query the nested field inside the `embeddedDocuments` type field specified in the `ancestorPath`. The query path must be a child of the `ancestorPath`, regardless of the level of nesting. This specifies the search criteria to filter the parent document. You can't use the `hasAncestor` operator inside the operator specification. | Required |

## Requirements  
To use this operator, you must:  
- Index the ancestor fields as the [embeddedDocuments](/docs/search/index/field-types/embedded-documents-type#std-label-bson-data-types-embedded-documents) type. In the query, specify `ancestorPath` as this field. If the field is on the root level, use [hasRoot.](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/hasRoot#std-label-has-root-ref)  
- Specify [returnScope](/docs/search/query/return-scope#std-label-fts-return-scope) to set the scope of the document to query and retrieve.

## Examples  
The examples in this section use the `sample_training.companies` dataset. If you load the sample dataset and create the index on the collection, you can try the sample queries demonstrated in this section.

# `hasRoot` Operator  
## Definition  
The `hasRoot` operator can be used to query root-level fields when you specify the `returnScope` and `returnStoredSource` options.

## Fields  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `operator` | Object | Operator to use to query an indexed field. This specifies the search criteria to filter the child documents. | Required |

## Requirements  
To use this operator, you must do the following in the index definition:  
- Index the root-level field that you want to query.  
- Index the array of objects that you want to retrieve as the `embeddedDocuments` type. You must also configure `storedSource` for nested fields that you want to retrieve.  
In the query, you must do the following:  
- Specify `returnScope` to set the scope of the field to search for the operator.  
- Set `returnStoredSource` to `true` to return the `storedSource` fields.

## Examples  
The examples in this section use the `sample_training.companies` namespace. If you load the sample dataset and create the index on the collection, you can try the sample queries demonstrated in this section.

### Simple Query  
The following query returns `products` where the root-level field `founded_year` is in between the years `2005` and `2010`.  
```javascript
db.companies.aggregate([
{
"$search": {
"returnStoredSource": true,
"returnScope": { "path": "products" },
"hasRoot": {
"operator": {
"range": {
"path": "founded_year",
"gte": 2005,
"lte": 2010
}
}
}
}
}
])

```

# `in` Operator  
## Definition  
The `in` operator in MongoDB Search performs a search for an array of BSON (Binary Javascript Object Notation) `number`, `date`, `boolean`, `objectId`, `uuid`, or `string` values at the given path and returns documents where the value of the field equals any value in the specified array. If the field holds an array, then the `in` operator selects the documents whose field holds an array that contains at least one element that matches any value in the specified array.

## Fields  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string or array of strings | Indexed field or fields to search. You can also specify a wildcard path to search. To search for [string](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/bson-types/#std-label-document-bson-type-string) values in a field, you must index the field as the MongoDB Search [token](/docs/search/index/field-types/token-type#std-label-bson-data-types-token) type. | Required |
| `score` | object | Score to assign to matching search term results. Use one of the following options to modify the score: `boost`: multiply the result score by the given number.; `constant`: replace the result score with the given number.; `function`: replace the result score using the function expression. | Optional |
| `value` | [boolean](/docs/search/index/field-types/boolean-type#std-label-boolean-ref), [objectId](/docs/search/index/field-types/object-id-type#std-label-objectId-ref), [number](/docs/search/index/field-types/number-type#std-label-bson-data-types-number), [date](/docs/search/index/field-types/date-type#std-label-bson-data-types-date), [uuid](/docs/search/index/field-types/uuid-type#std-label-bson-data-types-uuid), or [string](/docs/search/index/field-types/string-type#std-label-bson-data-types-string) | Value or values to search. Value can be either a single value or an array of values of only one of the supported BSON (Binary Javascript Object Notation) types and can't be a mix of different types. To search for [string](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/bson-types/#std-label-document-bson-type-string) values in a field, you must index the field as the MongoDB Search [token](/docs/search/index/field-types/token-type#std-label-bson-data-types-token) type. | Required |
| `doesNotAffect` | string or array of strings | Facet or list of facets to exclude from count recalculation on the basis of this query. Value must be one or more names of a facet defined in `$search.facets` or `$searchMeta.facets`. The operator uses the specified facets for filtering documents to match this query, but doesn't recalculate counts for them. For more information, see [Multi-Select Facets.](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/facet#std-label-fts-facet-multi-select) | Optional |

# `knnBeta` Operator  
The Atlas Search knnVector field type and knnBeta operator are now deprecated. Instead, we recommend that you use the [vector](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/search/field-types/vector-type/) index type and [vectorSearch](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/search/operators-collectors/vectorSearch/) operator in your $search pipeline stage.

## Definition  
The `knnBeta` operator uses the [Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320) algorithm to perform semantic search. You can use MongoDB Search support for kNN (K-nearest neighbors) queries to search for similar products, images, and other content.

## Options  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `filter` | document | Any MongoDB Search [operator](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/overview#std-label-operators-ref) to filter the documents based on metadata or certain search criteria, which can help narrow down the scope of vector search. | Optional |
| `k` | number | Number of nearest neighbors to return. You can specify a number higher than the number of documents to return ([`$limit`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/limit/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-limit)) to increase accuracy. | Required |
| `path` | string | Indexed [knnVector](/docs/search/index/field-types/knn-vector#std-label-fts-data-types-knn-vector) type field to search. | Required |
| `score` | document | Score assigned to matching documents in the results. To learn more, see [scoring behavior.](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/knn-beta#std-label-knn-beta-scoring) | Optional |
| `vector` | array of numbers | Array of numbers of BSON (Binary Javascript Object Notation) types `int` or `double` that represent the query vector. The array size must match the number of vector `dimensions` specified in the [index](/docs/search/index/field-types/knn-vector#std-label-fts-data-types-knn-vector) for the field. | Required |

### Performance  
To improve query performance, use the [`$project`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/project/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-project) stage to select the fields to return in the results, unless you need all the fields in the results. We recommend excluding the vector field in the [`$project`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/project/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-project) stage.

### Scoring  
You can use the `score` field with the [`$meta`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/meta/#mongodb-expression-exp.-meta) expression `searchScore` in the [`$project`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/project/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-project) stage to return the score for the documents in the results.  
MongoDB Search scores the results for kNN (K-nearest neighbors) queries in a fixed range from `0` to `1` only. For `cosine` and `dotProduct` [similarities](/docs/search/index/field-types/knn-vector#std-label-fts-knn-vector-type-options), MongoDB Search normalizes the score using the following algorithm:  
```shell
score = (1 + cosine/dot_product(v1,v2)) / 2
```

### Limitations  
`knnBeta` operator must be the top-level operator in your queries and therefore, you can't use the `knnBeta` operator inside the following:  
- [embeddedDocument](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/embedded-document#std-label-embedded-document-ref)  
- [compound](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/compound#std-label-compound-ref)  
- [`facet` (MongoDB Search Operator)](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/facet#std-label-fts-facet-ref)  
You can't use the `knnBeta` operator to query fields indexed using a [vectorSearch](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/vector-search/index/vector-search-type/#std-label-avs-types-vector-search) type index. You can't use the [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) [sort](/docs/search/query/sort#std-label-sort-ref) option with the `knnBeta` operator.  
We don't recommend paginating your MongoDB Search results using [`$skip`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/skip/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-skip) and [`$limit`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/limit/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-limit) after the [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) stage.

# `moreLikeThis` Operator  
## `moreLikeThis` Operator Limitations  
You can't use the `moreLikeThis` operator to query non-string values. To search for non-string values, you can combine a `moreLikeThis` query with a [near](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/near#std-label-near-ref), [range](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/range#std-label-range-ref), or any other operator in a [compound](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/compound#std-label-compound-ref) query.  
You can't use the `moreLikeThis` operator inside the [embeddedDocument](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/embedded-document#std-label-embedded-document-ref) to query documents in an array.

## Definition  
The `moreLikeThis` operator returns documents similar to input documents. The `moreLikeThis` operator allows you to build features for your applications that display similar or alternative results based on one or more given documents.

## Behavior  
When you run a `moreLikeThis` query, MongoDB Search performs these actions:  
- Extracts a limited number of most representative terms based on the input documents that you specify in the operator's `like` option.  
- Creates a disjunction (*OR*) query to find similar documents based on the most representative terms and returns the results.  
The `moreLikeThis` operator performs a search for similar documents using the [analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/overview#std-label-analyzers-ref) that you specify in the [index configuration](/docs/search/index/define-field-mappings#std-label-index-config-example). If you omit the analyzer in the index definition, the `moreLikeThis` operator uses the default [standard analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/standard#std-label-ref-standard-analyzer). If you specify multiple analyzers, the `moreLikeThis` operator runs the input text through each analyzer, searches, and returns results for all analyzers.  
To view the disjunction (*OR*) that MongoDB Search constructs to find similar documents, use [explain](/docs/search/query/explain#std-label-explain-ref) with your `moreLikeThis` operator query.

## Usage  
Before you can run the `moreLikeThis` operator query, we recommend that you retrieve one or more input documents. To retrieve input documents, you can do one of the following:  
- Run a query, such as [find()](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.find/), or another MQL query to find BSON (Binary Javascript Object Notation) documents.  
- Run any aggregation pipeline that returns BSON (Binary Javascript Object Notation) documents.  
- Use any other source of documents in your application.  
Once you identify the input documents, you can pass them to the `moreLikeThis` operator.  
When you run a `moreLikeThis` operator query, MongoDB Search returns the original input document in the query results. To omit the input document from the query results, use the `moreLikeThis` operator in a [compound](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/compound#std-label-compound-ref) operator query and exclude the input document by its `_id` using the `equals` operator in the [mustNot](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/compound#std-label-must-must-not-example-ref) clause.

## Options  
`moreLikeThis` uses the following option to constuct a query:  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `like` | one BSON (Binary Javascript Object Notation) document or an array of documents | One or more BSON (Binary Javascript Object Notation) documents that MongoDB Search uses to extract representative terms to query for. | Required |
| `score` | object | Score to assign to matching search results. You can modify the default score using the following options: `boost`: multiply the result score by the given number.; `constant`: replace the result score with the given number.; `function`: replace the result score with the given expression. For information on using `score` in your query, see [Score the Documents in the Results.](/docs/search/query/score/overview#std-label-scoring-ref) When querying array values, MongoDB Search assigns higher scores if more values in the array match the query. | Optional |

## Examples  
The examples use the `movies` collection in the `sample_mflix` database. Each example in this section uses a different index definition to demonstrate different features of the operator.  
Before you run the example queries on your cluster, [load the sample data](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/import/load-sample-data/#std-label-sample-data) on your cluster, and create the suggested index. To learn more about creating a MongoDB Search index using the UI, API, or CLI, see [Manage MongoDB Search Indexes](/docs/search/index/manage-indexes#std-label-ref-create-index). The index definitions use the name `default`.  
If you name your index `default`, you don't need to specify an `index` parameter in the [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) pipeline stage. If you give a custom name to your index, you must specify this name in the `index` parameter.

# `near` (MongoDB Search Operator)  
## `near` Operator Limitations  
You can't use the `near` operator to query numeric or date values stored in an array, even if you have a MongoDB Search index. You can use the [range](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/range#std-label-range-ref) only to query indexed numeric or date values inside arrays.

## Definition  
The `near` operator supports querying and scoring numeric, date, and GeoJSON point values. This operator can be used to perform a search over:  
- Number fields of BSON `int32`, `int64`, and `double` data types.  
- Date fields of BSON `date` type in :ISODate format.  
- Geographic location fields defined using latitude and longitude coordinates.  
You can use the `near` operator to find results that are near a number or a date. The `near` operator scores the MongoDB Search results by proximity to the number or date.

## Options  
`near` uses the following terms to construct a query:  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `origin` | date, number, or geo | Number, date, or geographic [point](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geojson-point) to search near. This is the origin from which the proximity of the results is measured. For number fields, the value must be of BSON `int32`, `int64`, or `double` data types.; For date fields, the value must be an :ISODate formatted date.; For [geo](/docs/search/index/field-types/geo-type#std-label-bson-data-types-geo) fields. the value must be a [GeoJSON point.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/geojson/#std-label-geojson-point) | yes |
| `path` | string or array of strings | Indexed field or fields to search. | yes |
| `pivot` | number | Value to use to calculate scores of MongoDB Search result documents. Score is calculated using the following formula: `              pivot
score = ------------------
pivot + distance` where `distance` is the difference between `origin` and the indexed field value. Results have a score equal to `1/2` (or `0.5`) when their indexed field value is `pivot` units away from `origin`. The value of `pivot` must be greater than (i.e. `>`) `0`. If `origin` is a: Number, `pivot` can be specified as an integer or floating point number.; Date, `pivot` must be specified in milliseconds and can be specified as a 32 or 64 bit integer. For example:1 minute is equal to `60,000 ms`; 1 hour is equal to `3,600,000 ms`; 1 day is equal to `86,400,000 ms`; 1 month (or 30 days) is equal to `2,592,000,000 ms`; GeoJSON point, `pivot` is measured in meters and must be specified as an integer or floating point number. | yes |
| `score` | object | Score to assign to matching search results. You can modify the default score using the following options: `boost`: multiply the result score by the given number.; `constant`: replace the result score with the given number.; `function`: replace the result score with the given expression. For information on using `score` in your query, see [Score the Documents in the Results.](/docs/search/query/score/overview#std-label-scoring-ref) To learn more, see [Scoring Behavior.](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/near#std-label-near-query-score) | no |

## Scoring Behavior  
MongoDB Search `score` is a measure of the proximity of the MongoDB Search results to `origin`. The `score` is scaled between `0` and `1` with `1` being an exact match and `0` being a distant match. Score is equal to `0.5` when the distance of the MongoDB Search result from `origin` is equal to the distance away from origin as calculated using `pivot`.  
The `near` operator uses the following distance decay function to calculate document score:  
```text
pivot
score = ------------------
pivot + distance
```  
where each term is defined as follows:  
| Factor | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `pivot` | Value specified as a reference point to make the score equal to `0.5` if the distance between `fieldValue` and `origin` is equal to it. This defines how quickly the score decays as the distance between `fieldValue` and `origin` grows. For a given distance between `fieldValue` and `origin`, if `pivot` decreases, the score also decreases. |
| `distance` | Absolute distance between `fieldValue` and `origin`. MongoDB Search computes this value using the following formula: `abs(fieldValue - origin)` where: `fieldValue` is the value of the field that you are querying in the document.; `origin` is the number, date, or geographic point to search near. |  
You can modify the default score using  `score` option in your query. To learn more about the options, [Modify the Score.](/docs/search/query/score/modify-score#std-label-scoring-options)

# `phrase` (MongoDB Search Operator)  
## Definition  
The `phrase` operator performs search for documents containing an ordered sequence of terms using the [analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/overview#std-label-analyzers-ref) specified in the [index configuration](/docs/search/index/define-field-mappings#std-label-index-config-example). If no analyzer is specified, the default [standard](/docs/search/index/analyzers/standard#std-label-ref-standard-analyzer) analyzer is used.  
You can use the `phrase` operator to search for exact matches to multi-word phrases.

## Options  
`phrase` uses the following terms to construct a query:  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `query` | string or array of strings | String or strings to search for. | yes |
| `path` | string or array of strings | Indexed field or fields to search. You can also specify a wildcard path to search. IMPORTANT: To use the `phrase` operator, you must index the query field as type `string` with the `indexOptions` property set to `positions` or the default value, `offsets`. To learn more, see [Configure String Field Properties.](/docs/search/index/field-types/string-type#std-label-fts-field-types-string-options) | yes |
| `slop` | integer | Allowable distance between words in the `query` phrase. Lower value allows less positional distance between the words and greater value allows more reorganization of the words and more distance between the words to satisfy the query. The default is `0`, meaning that words must be exactly in the same position as the query to be considered a match. Exact matches are scored higher. | no |
| `score` | object | Score to assign to matching search results. You can modify the default score using the following options: `boost`: multiply the result score by the given number.; `constant`: replace the result score with the given number.; `function`: replace the result score with the given expression. When querying array values, MongoDB Search assigns higher scores if more values in the array match the query. For information on the options for modifying the default score, see [Score the Documents in the Results.](/docs/search/query/score/overview#std-label-scoring-ref) | no |
| `synonyms` | string | Required for running queries using [synonyms.](/docs/search/index/synonyms#std-label-synonyms-ref) Name of the [synonym mapping definition](/docs/search/index/synonyms#std-label-synonyms-ref) in the [index definition](/docs/search/index/index-definitions#std-label-ref-index-definitions). Value can't be an empty string. The amount of time that MongoDB Search takes to execute queries that use [synonym mappings](/docs/search/index/synonyms#std-label-synonyms-ref) depends on the number and size of documents in the synonym source collection. For example, a query that uses a synonym mapping that is based on very few synonym documents might be faster than a query that uses a synonym mapping that is based on many synonym documents. | Optional |

## Scoring Behavior  
By default, the [text](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/text#std-label-text-ref) operator uses the `bm25` similarity algorithm to score documents depending on their relevance to the query.  
You can change which similarity algorithm is used by specifying a different similarity algorithm in the `similarity.type` property for the `string` fields in your MongoDB Search index definition. To learn how to configure a MongoDB Search index for the `string` type, see [How to Index String Fields](/docs/search/index/field-types/string-type#std-label-bson-data-types-string).  
To learn more about the supported similarity algorithms, see [Score Details.](/docs/search/query/score/get-details#std-label-fts-similarity-algorithms)

## Examples  
The examples in this page use the `movies` collection in the `sample_mflix` database. After loading the [sample dataset](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/sample-data/#std-label-available-sample-datasets) into your cluster, create the MongoDB Search index with dynamic mappings and run the example queries on your cluster. To try the [synonyms](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/text#std-label-text-ref-synonyms-eg) examples, you must also add the [synonymous\_terms collection](/docs/search/index/synonyms#std-label-sample-synonyms-coll) to the `sample_mflix` database and then [define the index](/docs/search/index/synonyms#std-label-synonyms-index-definition-ex) with the `synonyms` mapping collection.
The results show that there are 3 movies between 2000 and 2005, 8 movies between 2005 and 2010, and 4 movies between 2010 and 2015 that contain the term `new york` in the `title`.

# `queryString` Operator  
## Definition  
The `queryString` operator supports querying a combination of indexed fields and values. You can perform text, wildcard, regular expression, fuzzy, and range searches on `string` fields using the `queryString` operator.

## Options  
`queryString` uses the following terms to construct a query:  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `defaultPath` | string | The indexed field to search by default. MongoDB Search only searches the field in `defaultPath` if you omit the field to search in the `query`. | yes |
| `query` | string | One or more indexed fields and values to search. Fields and values are colon-delimited. For example, to search the `plot` field for the string `baseball`, use `plot:baseball`. The following operators are available to combine multiple search criteria: You can combine the fields and values using the following: `AND`Indicates `AND` boolean operator. All search values must be present for a document to be included in the results.`OR`Indicates `OR` boolean operator. At least one of the search value must be present for a document to be included in the results.`NOT`Indicates `NOT` boolean operator. Specified search value must be absent for a document to be included in the results.`TO`Indicates the range to search. You can use `[]` for an inclusive range, `{}` for an exclusive range, or `{]` and `[}` for an half-open range. Any value that falls within the specified range must be present for a document to be included in the results.`()`Delimiters for subqueries. Use the parentheses to group fields and values to search. You can run wildcard and regular expression queries using the following: `?`Indicates any single character to match.`*`Indicates 0 or more characters to match.The `queryString` operator doesn't support a wildcard query with `*` as the first character in the query. The `queryString` operator treats any character preceding the `*` as prefix or as characters that must exactly match.`/`Delimiter for regular expression.`~`Indicates fuzzy search to find strings which are similar to the search term by up to the specified number of edits. For example, `{ "query":"foo":"stop"~2 }` is equal to the following:`{ "defaultPath": "foo", "query": "stop", "maxEdits": 2 }`The `queryString` operator only supports fuzzy search for up to at most 2 edits. Higher distances are not useful as the results may match many dictionary terms.If you use `~` with multiple terms in a string, the `queryString` operator does a proximity search for the terms within the specified number of terms. For example, `{ "query":"foo":"New York"~2 }` is equal to the following:`{ "defaultPath": "foo", "query": "New York", "slop": 2 }` | yes | | `score` | object | The score assigned to matching search results. You can modify the default score using the following options: `boost`: multiply the result score by the given number.; `constant`: replace the result score with the given number.; `function`: replace the result score with the given expression. When querying array values, MongoDB Search assigns higher scores if more values in the array match the query. For information on using `score` in your query, see [Score the Documents in the Results.](/docs/search/query/score/overview#std-label-scoring-ref) | no |

## Scoring Behavior  
By default, the [text](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/text#std-label-text-ref) operator uses the `bm25` similarity algorithm to score documents depending on their relevance to the query.  
You can change which similarity algorithm is used by specifying a different similarity algorithm in the `similarity.type` property for the `string` fields in your MongoDB Search index definition. To learn how to configure a MongoDB Search index for the `string` type, see [How to Index String Fields](/docs/search/index/field-types/string-type#std-label-bson-data-types-string).  
To learn more about the supported similarity algorithms, see [Score Details.](/docs/search/query/score/get-details#std-label-fts-similarity-algorithms)

The following examples use the `movies` collection in the `sample_mflix` database. If you have the [sample dataset](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/sample-data/#std-label-available-sample-datasets) on your cluster , you can create the MongoDB Search index named `default` with dynamic mappings and run the example queries on your cluster.

### Range Queries

### TO  
The following example uses the `queryString` operator to query the movie titles a range of textual values from the characters `count` to any character (defined using the wildcard character `*`) in ascending alphabetical order.  
```json
db.movies.aggregate([
{
"$search": {
"queryString": {
"defaultPath": "plot",
"query": "title:[count TO *]"
}
}
},
{
"$limit": 10
},
{
"$project": {
"_id": 0,
"title": 1
}
}
])
```  
**Output:**  
```json
[
{ title: 'Blacksmith Scene' },
{ title: 'The Great Train Robbery' },
{ title: 'The Land Beyond the Sunset' },
{ title: 'A Corner in Wheat' },
{ title: 'Winsor McCay, the Famous Cartoonist of the N.Y. Herald and His Moving Comics' },
{ title: 'Traffic in Souls' },
{ title: 'Gertie the Dinosaur' },
{ title: 'In the Land of the Head Hunters' },
{ title: 'The Perils of Pauline' },
{ title: 'The Birth of a Nation' }
]
```  
MongoDB Search results include movies with titles `Blacksmith Scene` and `A Corner in Wheat` although the range in the query starts from characters `count`. When you index with the default analyzer, `lucene.standard`, MongoDB Search creates separate tokens for the terms in the `title` field and matches the query term to the individual tokens. Specifically, MongoDB Search creates the following tokens, at least one of which (indicated by √) matches the query criteria:  
| Title | Standard Analyzer Tokens |
| --- | --- |
| Blacksmith Scene | `blacksmith`, `scene` √ |
| A Corner in Wheat | `a`, `corner`, `in`, `wheat` √ |  
If you index using the `lucene.keyword` analyzer, MongoDB Search would create a single token for the whole string in the `title` field, resulting in results similar to the following for the same query:  
```json
[
{ title: 'è Nous la Libertè' },
{ title: 'tom thumb' },
{ title: 'è nos amours' },
{ title: 'èke och hans vèrld' },
{ title: 'èdipussi' },
{ title: 's/y Glèdjen' },
{ title: 'èAy, Carmela!' },
{ title: 'èlisa' },
{ title: 'èxtasis' },
{ title: 'eXistenZ' }
]
```

# `range` (MongoDB Search Operator)  
## Definition  
The `range` operator supports querying and scoring numeric, date, and string values. You can use this operator to find results that are within a given numeric, date, objectId, or letter (from the English alphabet) range.  
`range` supports querying the following data types:  
- [number](/docs/search/index/field-types/number-type#std-label-bson-data-types-number), including `int32`, `int64`, and `double`  
- [date](/docs/search/index/field-types/date-type#std-label-bson-data-types-date)  
- [string](/docs/search/index/field-types/string-type#std-label-bson-data-types-string), indexed as MongoDB Search [token](/docs/search/index/field-types/token-type#std-label-bson-data-types-token) type  
- [objectId](/docs/search/index/field-types/object-id-type#std-label-objectId-ref)

## Options  
`range` uses the following terms to construct a query:  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gt` or `gte` | BSON date, number, or string, or objectId | Find values greater than (`>`) or greater than or equal to (`>=`) the given value. For number fields, the value can be an `int32`, `int64`, or `double` data type.; For date fields, the value must be an :ISODate formatted date.; For string fields, the value must be indexed as MongoDB Search `token` type.; For `ObjectId` fields, the value must be indexed as [objectId](/docs/search/index/field-types/object-id-type#std-label-objectId-ref) data type or [dynamic mappings](/docs/search/index/define-field-mappings#std-label-static-dynamic-mappings) must be set to `true`. | no |
| `lt` or `lte` | BSON date, number, or string, or objectId | Find values less than (`<`) or less than or equal to (`<=`) the given value. For number fields, the value can be an `int32`, `int64`, or `double` data type.; For date fields, the value must be an :ISODate formatted date.; For string fields, the value must be indexed as MongoDB Search `token` type.; For `ObjectId` fields, the value must be indexed as [objectId](/docs/search/index/field-types/object-id-type#std-label-objectId-ref) data type or [dynamic mappings](/docs/search/index/define-field-mappings#std-label-static-dynamic-mappings) must be set to `true`. | no |
| `path` | string or array of strings | Indexed field or fields to search. | yes |
| `score` | object | Modify the score assigned to matching search results. You can modify the default score using the following options: `boost`: multiply the result score by the given number.; `constant`: replace the result score with the given number.; `function`: replace the result score with the given expression. When querying array values, MongoDB Search assigns higher scores if more values in the array match the query. For information on using `score` in your query, see [Score the Documents in the Results.](/docs/search/query/score/overview#std-label-scoring-ref) | no |
| `doesNotAffect` | string or array of strings | Facet or list of facets to exclude from count recalculation on the basis of this query. Value must be one or more names of a facet defined in `$search.facets` or `$searchMeta.facets`. The operator uses the specified facets for filtering documents to match this query, but doesn't recalculate counts for them. For more information, see [Multi-Select Facets.](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/facet#std-label-fts-facet-multi-select) | no |

# `regex` (MongoDB Search Operator)  
## Definition  
`regex` interprets the `query` field as a regular expression. `regex` is a term-level operator, meaning that the `query` field isn't analyzed.  
**See also:**  
- [Analyzers.](/docs/search/index/analyzers/overview#std-label-analyzers-ref)  
- [Analyzed field example.](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/regex#std-label-analyzed-field-example)  
**Note:**  
The regular expression language available to the `regex` operator is a limited subset of the PCRE (Perl Compatible Regular Expressions) library.  
For detailed information, see the [Class RegExp](https://lucene.apache.org/core/8_0_0/core/org/apache/lucene/util/automaton/RegExp.html) documentation.

## Options  
`regex` uses the following terms to construct a query:  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `query` | string or array of strings | String or strings to search for. | yes | |
| `path` | string or array of strings | Indexed field or fields to search. You can also specify a wildcard path to search. | yes | |
| `allowAnalyzedField` | boolean | Must be set to `true` if the query is run against an analyzed field. | no | `false` |
| `score` | object | [Score](/docs/search/query/score/overview#std-label-scoring-ref) to assign to matching search term results. Options are: `boost`: multiply the result score by the given number.; `constant`: replace the result score with the given number.; `function`: replace the result score with the given expression. | no | |

## Behavior  
`regex` is a term-level operator, meaning that the `query` field is not analyzed. Regular expression searches work well with the [keyword analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/keyword#std-label-ref-keyword-analyzer), because it indexes fields one word at a time. To do a case-sensitive search, do not use the default analyzer, [standard analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/standard#std-label-ref-standard-analyzer), because the `standard` analyzer lower cases all terms. Specify a different [analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/overview#std-label-analyzers-ref) instead.  
It is possible to use the `regex` operator to perform searches on an analyzed field by setting the `allowAnalyzedField` option to `true`, but you may get unexpected results.  
**Example:**  
Searching for `.*Star Trek.*` on a field indexed with the [keyword analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/keyword#std-label-ref-keyword-analyzer) finds all documents in which the field contains the string `Star Trek` in any context. Searching for `.*Star
Trek.*` on a field indexed with the [standard analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/standard#std-label-ref-standard-analyzer) finds nothing, because there is a space between `Star` and `Trek`, and the index contains no spaces.

## Lucene Regular Expression Behavior  
The MongoDB Search `regex` operator uses the [Lucene regular expression engine](https://lucene.apache.org/core/8_0_0/core/org/apache/lucene/util/automaton/RegExp.html), which differs from [Perl Compatible Regular Expressions.](https://www.pcre.org/)

### Reserved characters  
The following characters are reserved as operators when used in regular expressions:  
`. ? + * | { } [ ] ( ) < > " \ @ #`  
To use any of the above characters literally in a matching expression, precede it with a `\` character.  
**Example:**  
`who\?` *matches "who?"*  
When using the escape character in [`mongosh`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongodb-shell/#mongodb-binary-bin.mongosh) or with a [driver](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/), you must use a double backslash before the character to be escaped.  
**Example:**  
To create a wildcard expression which searches for any string containing a literal asterisk in an aggregation pipeline, use the following expression:  
```none
"*\\**"
```  
The first and last asterisks act as wildcards which match any characters, and the `\\*` matches a literal asterisk.  
Use the following expression to escape a literal backslash:  
```none
"*\\\*"
```

### Supported Operators  
| Operator | Description | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.` | Matches any character. | `x.z` *matches "xyz", "xaz", etc.* |
| `?` | The preceding character is optional and matches if it occurs no more than once. | `xyz?` *matches "xy" and "xyz"* |
| `+` | The preceding character matches if it occurs one or more times. | `xy+` *matches "xy", "xyy", "xyyy", etc.* |
| `*` | The preceding character matches if it occurs any number of times. | `xyz*` *matches "xy", "xyz", "xyzz", etc.* |
| `|` | The `OR` operator. The expression matches if either of the two patterns on either side of the `|` operator matches. | `abc|xyz` *matches "abc" or "xyz"* |
| `{<number>}` | The preceding character matches if it occurs exactly <number> times. | `xyz{3}` *matches "xyzzz"* |
| `()` | Characters inside parentheses are treated as a single unit for matching purposes. | `xyz(abc)[2]` *matches "xyzabcabc"* |
| `[]` | Matches any of the characters inside the square brackets. Adding a `^` to the beginning matches any character except those within the square brackets. Inside the square brackets, `-` indicates a range, unless `-` is the first character or is escaped with a `\`. | `[xyz]` *matches "x", "y", and "z"*`[^abc]` *matches any character except "a", "b", or "c"*`[a-d]` *matches "a", "b", "c", or "d"*`[0-9]` *matches any numeric character from 0 through 9* |
| `<>` | Match a numeric range. | `<1-3>` *matches "1", "2", and "3"* |
| `#` | The empty language operator. The `#` operator does not match any string, including an empty string. | `#|xyz` *matches "xyz" and nothing else* |

### Unsupported Operators  
`regex` does not support anchor operators. For example, these operators are not supported:  
- `^`, which matches the beginning of a line.  
- `$`, which matches the end of a line.  
To match a term, the regular expression must match the entire string.

# `span` (MongoDB Search Operator)  
## Definition  
**Note:**  
The `span` operator is deprecated. Instead, use the [phrase.](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/phrase#std-label-phrase-ref)  
The `span` operator finds text search matches within regions of a text field. You can use it to find strings which are near each other to specified degrees of precision. The `span` operator is more computationally intensive than other operators, because queries must keep track of positional information.  
`span` is a term-level operator, which means that the `query` field is not analyzed. Term-level operators work well with the [Keyword Analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/keyword#std-label-ref-keyword-analyzer) because the `query` field is treated as a single term, with special characters included.  
`span` queries aren't ranked by score.

## Term Operator  
You can use the `term` operator to specify the terms to search. The `term` operator is required and when you use it with `span` [positional](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/span#std-label-span-positional-operators-ref) operators, it must be the innermost child of the positional operators.

### Syntax  
The `term` operator has the following syntax:  
```json
"term": {
"path": "<path-to-field>",
"query": "<terms-to-search>"
}
```

### Fields  
The `term` operator takes the following fields:  
| Option | Type | Required? | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string | yes | Indexed field to search. |
| `query` | string | yes | Term or phrase to search. |

## Positional Operators  
You can use the positional operators to specify the position of the terms that you want to search with the [term](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/span#std-label-span-term-ref) operator. The positional operators are of type `document`. You must specify at least one positional operator in your `span` operator query. The positional operators can take other `span` positional operators, recursively.  
**Note: About the Examples**  
The examples on this page use the `sample_mflix.movies` collection. If you [load the sample data](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/import/load-sample-data/#std-label-sample-data) and [create](/docs/search/index/manage-indexes#std-label-ref-create-index) a [dynamic](/docs/search/index/define-field-mappings#std-label-static-dynamic-mappings) index named `default` on the [movies collection](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/sample-data/sample-mflix/#std-label-sample-mflix) , you can run the following [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) sample queries against the collection. The sample queries use the [`$limit`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/limit/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-limit) stage to limit the results to `5` documents and the [`$project`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/project/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-project) stage to exclude all fields except the `title` field in the results.  
`span` takes the following optional positional operators.

# `text` (MongoDB Search Operator)  
## Definition  
The `text` operator performs a full-text search using the [analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/overview#std-label-analyzers-ref) that you specify in the [index configuration](/docs/search/index/define-field-mappings#std-label-index-config-example). If you omit an analyzer, the `text` operator uses the default [standard](/docs/search/index/analyzers/standard#std-label-ref-standard-analyzer) analyzer.  
You can use the `text` operator to search for exact matches to single-word terms.

## Options  
`text` uses the following terms to construct a query:  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `query` | string or array of strings | The string or strings to search for. If there are multiple terms in a string, MongoDB Search also looks for a match for each term in the string separately. | Required |
| `path` | string or array of strings | The indexed field or fields to search. You can also specify a wildcard path to search. | Required |
| `fuzzy` | document | Enable fuzzy search. Find strings which are similar to the search term or terms. You can't use `fuzzy` with `synonyms`. | Optional |
| `fuzzy.maxEdits` | integer | Maximum number of single-character edits required to match the specified search term. Value can be `1` or `2`. The default value is `2`. Uses [Damerau-Levenshtein distance.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damerau%E2%80%93Levenshtein_distance) | Optional |
| `fuzzy.prefixLength` | integer | Number of characters at the beginning of each term in the result that must exactly match. The default value is `0`. | Optional |
| `fuzzy.maxExpansions` | integer | Maximum number of variations to generate and search for. This limit applies on a per-token basis. The default value is `50`. | Optional |
| `matchCriteria` | string | Criteria to use to match the terms in the query. If omitted, defaults to `any`. Value can be one of the following: `any` - to return documents that contain any of the terms from the `query` field.; `all` - to only return documents that contain all of the terms from the `query` field. | Optional, Recommended |
| `score` | document | Score assigned to matching search term results. Use one of the following options to modify the score: `boost`: multiply the result score by the given number.; `constant`: replace the result score with the given number.; `function`: replace the result score using the given expression. When querying array values, MongoDB Search assigns higher scores if more values in the array match the query. | Optional |
| `synonyms` | string | Required for running queries using [synonyms.](/docs/search/index/synonyms#std-label-synonyms-ref) Name of the [synonym mapping definition](/docs/search/index/synonyms#std-label-synonyms-ref) in the [index definition](/docs/search/index/index-definitions#std-label-ref-index-definitions). Value can't be an empty string. You can't use `fuzzy` with `synonyms`. IMPORTANT: To use the `synonyms` option, you must index the query field as type `string` with the `indexOptions` property set to `positions` or the default value, `offsets`. To learn more, see [Configure String Field Properties.](/docs/search/index/field-types/string-type#std-label-fts-field-types-string-options) Always use `matchCriteria` when using `synonyms`. For `text` queries that use `synonyms` without `matchCriteria`, MongoDB Search only matches documents where all the terms are exactly in the same position as the query. This behavior might change in the future and your query results might also change. The amount of time that MongoDB Search takes to execute queries that use [synonym mappings](/docs/search/index/synonyms#std-label-synonyms-ref) depends on the number and size of documents in the synonym source collection. A query that uses a synonym mapping that is based on very few synonym documents might be faster than a query that uses a synonym mapping that is based on many synonym documents. | Optional |

## Scoring Behavior  
By default, the [text](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/text#std-label-text-ref) operator uses the `bm25` similarity algorithm to score documents depending on their relevance to the query.  
You can change which similarity algorithm is used by specifying a different similarity algorithm in the `similarity.type` property for the `string` fields in your MongoDB Search index definition. To learn how to configure a MongoDB Search index for the `string` type, see [How to Index String Fields](/docs/search/index/field-types/string-type#std-label-bson-data-types-string).  
To learn more about the supported similarity algorithms, see [Score Details.](/docs/search/query/score/get-details#std-label-fts-similarity-algorithms)

## Behavior  
For `text` queries that use `synonyms` without `matchCriteria`, MongoDB Search only matches documents which contain an exact match of the query terms (with or without the expanded synonyms).  
This behavior might change in the future and your query results might also change. To avoid service disruptions, always use `matchCriteria` when using `synonyms`. Or, use synonyms with the [phrase](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/phrase#std-label-phrase-ref) operator.  
For example, suppose equivalent synonym mappings for `nyc` and `new
york city`. A search for `i like nyc` returns the following:  
| Operator Specification | Default Behavior | `"matchCriteria": "any"` | `"matchCriteria": "all"` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `text` without `synonyms` | Matches `i` OR `like` OR `nyc` | Matches `i` OR `like` OR `nyc` | Matches `i` AND `like` AND `nyc` |
| `text` with `synonyms` | Matches `i like nyc` OR `i like new york city` | Matches `i` OR `like` OR (`nyc` OR `new york city`) | Matches `i` AND `like` AND (`nyc` OR `new york city`) |  
The amount of time that MongoDB Search takes to execute queries that use [synonym mappings](/docs/search/index/synonyms#std-label-synonyms-ref) depends on the number and size of documents in the synonym source collection. A query that uses a synonym mapping that is based on very few synonym documents might be faster than a query that uses a synonym mapping that is based on many synonym documents.

The examples in this page use the `movies` collection in the `sample_mflix` database. After loading the [sample dataset](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/sample-data/#std-label-available-sample-datasets) into your cluster, create the MongoDB Search index with dynamic mappings and run the example queries on your cluster. # `wildcard` Operator  
## Definition  
The `wildcard` operator enables queries which use special characters in the search string that can match any character.  
| Character | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `?` | Matches any single character. |
| `*` | Matches 0 or more characters. |
| `\` | Escape character. |  
`wildcard` is a term-level operator, meaning that the `query` field is not analyzed. Term-level operators work well with the [Keyword Analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/keyword#std-label-ref-keyword-analyzer), because the `query` field is treated as a single term, with special characters included. For an example of querying against an analyzed `query` field, see the [analyzed field example.](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/wildcard#std-label-analyzed-example)

## Options  
`wildcard` uses the following terms to construct a query:  
| Field | Type | Description | Necessity | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `query` | string or array of strings | String or strings to search for. | yes | |
| `path` | string or array of strings | Indexed field or fields to search. You can also specify a wildcard path to search. | yes | |
| `allowAnalyzedField` | boolean | Set to `true` if you run your query against a field indexed with a tokenizing analyzer. This avoids the field's analyzer from splitting the indexed value into many terms. Fields indexed with the [Keyword Analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/keyword#std-label-ref-keyword-analyzer) don't require this option. | no | `false` |
| `score` | object | Modify the [score](/docs/search/query/score/overview#std-label-scoring-ref) assigned to matching search term results. Options are: `boost`: multiply the result score by the given number.; `constant`: replace the result score with the given number.; `function`: replace the result score using the given expression. For information on using `score` in your query, see [Score the Documents in the Results.](/docs/search/query/score/overview#std-label-scoring-ref) | no | |

## Behavior  
`wildcard` is a term-level operator, meaning that the `query` field isn't analyzed. Use the `wildcard` operator on fields indexed with tokenizing analyzers by setting `allowAnalyzedField` to `true`. Fields indexed with the [Keyword Analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/keyword#std-label-ref-keyword-analyzer) already treat the field value as a single term, so `allowAnalyzedField: true` isn't required.  
If you use `wildcard` with `allowAnalyzedField: true`, MongoDB Search applies character filters and token filters based on the specified analyzer or custom analyzer for the field. MongoDB Search skips the tokenization and the output is always a single token.  
The following examples show how the `wildcard` operator behaves when performing a search on analyzed fields:  
**Example:**

### Standard Analyzer  
Suppose that a field `foo bar baz` is indexed with the [standard analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/standard#std-label-ref-standard-analyzer). MongoDB Search analyzes and indexes the field as  `foo`, `bar` and `baz`. Searching for `foo bar*` on this field finds nothing, because the wildcard operator treats `foo bar*` as a single search term with a wildcard at the end. In other words, MongoDB Search searches the field for any term that begins with `foo bar` but finds nothing, because no term exists.  
**Example:**

### Keyword Analyzer  
Searching for `*Star Trek*` on a field indexed with the [keyword analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/keyword#std-label-ref-keyword-analyzer) finds all documents in which the field contains the string `Star Trek` in any context. Searching for `*Star
Trek*` on a field indexed with the [standard analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/standard#std-label-ref-standard-analyzer) finds nothing, because there is a space between `Star` and `Trek`, and the index contains no spaces.

### Escape Character Behavior  
When using the escape character in [`mongosh`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongodb-shell/#mongodb-binary-bin.mongosh) or with a [driver](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/), you must use a double backslash before the character to be escaped.  
**Example:**  
To create a wildcard expression which searches for any string containing a literal asterisk in an aggregation pipeline, use the following expression:  
```none
"*\\**"
```  
The first and last asterisks act as wildcards which match any characters, and the `\\*` matches a literal asterisk.  
Use the following expression to escape a literal backslash:  
```none
"*\\\*"
```

# Paginate the Results  
On clusters running MongoDB 7.0.5+, use MongoDB Search to retrieve your [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query results sequentially after or before a reference point. Use the [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) `searchAfter` or `searchBefore` options to traverse results in-order and build "Next Page" and "Previous Page" functions in your application.

## Usage  
To retrieve paginated results, perform the following steps:  
[Create an index](/docs/search/index/manage-indexes#std-label-ref-create-index) on the fields you want to query.  
Run a [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query that returns a point of reference. To learn more, see [Retrieve Point of Reference.](/docs/search/query/paginate-results#std-label-paginate-results-search-sequence-token)  
Use the point of reference in your subsequent [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query to retrieve the next or previous set of documents in the results.  
- To learn more about retrieving results to build a "Next Page" function, see [Search After a Specific Point of Reference.](/docs/search/query/paginate-results#std-label-paginate-results-search-after)  
- To learn more about retrieving results to build a "Previous Page" function, see [Search Before a Specific Point of Reference.](/docs/search/query/paginate-results#std-label-paginate-results-search-before)  
- To jump to a page in your results, combine [`$skip`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/skip/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-skip) and [`$limit`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/limit/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-limit) with [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) `searchAfter` or `searchBefore` options. For example, to jump to results from Page 3 to Page 5, with 10 results per page, do the following:  
Retrieve results using `searchAfter` with the point of reference for the last result on Page 3 (Result 30).  
Use [`$skip`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/skip/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-skip) to skip the 10 results on Page 4 (Results 31-40) and [`$limit`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/limit/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-limit) to limit the results to 10 documents.  
Return results for Page 5 (Results 41-50).  
Here, using [`$skip`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/skip/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-skip) with the `searchAfter` option optimizes the query to skip only 1 page of results (10 documents). By comparison, if you use `$skip` without the [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) `searchAfter` option, the query skips 4 pages of results (40 documents). To learn more, see [Jump from Page 2 to Page 5 Using searchAfter and $skip.](/docs/search/query/paginate-results#std-label-sequential-pagination-tutorial-skip-query)

## Considerations  
- A tie occurs when you sort on a field for which multiple documents have identical values. MongoDB doesn't guarantee ordering of tied query results, which can lead to duplication and inconsistency when you use `searchAfter` and `searchBefore`. Apply the following principles to reduce relevance score ties:  
- Sort your query by a unique field to prevent relevance score ties. For an example, see [Sort by Score And a Unique Field.](/docs/search/query/sort#std-label-fts-sort-score-unique-field)  
- If you want to primarily sort by a non-unique field, add a secondary sort clause on a unique field to serve as a tiebreaker.  
- Updating or deleting documents between queries might cause inconsistencies in result order. Apply the following principles to support deterministic search behavior:  
- Sort your query results by an immutable field, such as `_id`. MongoDB Search reflects the updates you make to your collection between initial and subsequent queries. If you sort by a mutable field such as `updated_time` and you update your collection between your first and second queries, MongoDB Search might order the same documents differently.  
- If you deployed [dedicated Search nodes](/docs/search/deployment/deployment-options#std-label-node-architecture) and you are sorting results by `searchScore`, consider the following:
- By default, MongoDB Search scores documents using the `bm25` similarity algorithm, which calculates term frequency in relation to the entire corpus of documents on the MongoDB Search node. Because each MongoDB Search node replicates from the changestream independently, this corpus might vary across MongoDB Search nodes. As a result, the same query can return different `bm25` scores when routed to different MongoDB Search nodes. Subsequent queries are more likely to be routed to different MongoDB Search nodes if your deployment uses [dedicated MongoDB Search nodes](/docs/search/deployment/deployment-options#std-label-node-architecture), or your [read preference](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/read-preference/) is set to `secondary` or `nearest`.  
- To ensure consistent scores across subsequent queries, set the `similarity.type` property to `stableTfl` or `boolean` when you index a field as the MongoDB Search [string](/docs/search/index/field-types/string-type#std-label-bson-data-types-string) or [autocomplete](/docs/search/index/field-types/autocomplete-type#std-label-bson-data-types-autocomplete) type. This forces the [text](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/text#std-label-text-ref), [phrase](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/phrase#std-label-phrase-ref), [queryString](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/queryString#std-label-querystring-ref), and [autocomplete](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/autocomplete#std-label-autocomplete-ref) operators to use the `stableTfl` or `boolean` similarity algorithm to calculate relevance scores for queries on the indexed field. These algorithms calculate scores consistently across all MongoDB Search nodes. To learn more, see [Score Details.](/docs/search/query/score/get-details#std-label-fts-similarity-algorithms)  
- To count search results during pagination, use the [count](/docs/search/query/counting#std-label-count-ref) option in your initial [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query or in a separate [`$searchMeta`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/searchMeta#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-searchMeta) query. This method is more efficient than using the [`$count`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/count/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-count) stage after your [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) stage.  
The [count](/docs/search/query/counting#std-label-count-ref) option returns the total number of documents that match your search criteria, so you don't need to use the `count` option in later queries if you are generating paginated results. To keep counting separate from your main `$search` query, use a [`$searchMeta`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/searchMeta#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-searchMeta) stage with the `count` option.  
Counting search results can affect performance. Use the [count](/docs/search/query/counting#std-label-count-ref) option only when needed, for example, when retrieving search results for the first page.

## Retrieve Point of Reference  
To retrieve query results at a certain point, you must provide the point of reference in your [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query. You can retrieve the reference point by using the [`$meta`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/meta/#mongodb-expression-exp.-meta) keyword `searchSequenceToken` in the [`$project`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/project/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-project) stage after your [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) stage.

### Output  
The `searchSequenceToken` generates a Base64-encoded token for each document in the results. The length of the token increases with the number of fields specified in the [sort](/docs/search/query/sort#std-label-sort-ref) option of your query. The token isn't tied to a snapshot of the database.  
The documents in the results are sorted in the default order, unless you specify the `sort` option in your query. To learn about sorting your results, see [Sort MongoDB Search Results.](/docs/search/query/sort#std-label-sort-ref)

## Search After a Specific Point of Reference  
To search after a reference point, you must specify the reference point in your [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query by using the `searchAfter` option with the token generated by `searchSequenceToken`. You can use the token generated by `searchSequenceToken` only when you rerun the [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query for which `searchSequenceToken` generated the token. The semantics (search fields and values) of the subsequent [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query in which you use the token must be identical to the query for which `searchSequenceToken` generated the token.  
You can use the `searchAfter` option to build a "Next Page" function in your application. For a demonstration of this, see the [example](/docs/search/query/paginate-results#std-label-search-before-egs) on this page.

### Output  
MongoDB Search returns the documents in the results after the specified token. MongoDB Search returns the generated tokens for the documents in the results because you specified the `searchSequenceToken` in the [`$project`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/project/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-project) stage after the [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) stage (as shown in line 11). These tokens can be used as a reference point for another query with the same semantics.  
The documents in the results are sorted in the default order, unless you specify the `sort` option in your query. To learn about sorting your results, see [Sort MongoDB Search Results.](/docs/search/query/sort#std-label-sort-ref)

## Search Before a Specific Point of Reference  
To search before a reference point, you must specify the reference point in your [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query by using the `searchBefore` option with the token generated by `searchSequenceToken`. You can use the token generated by `searchSequenceToken` only when you rerun the [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query for which `searchSequenceToken` generated the token. The semantics (search fields and values) of the subsequent [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) query in which you use the token must be identical to the query for which `searchSequenceToken` generated the token.  
You can use the `searchBefore` option to build a "Previous Page" function in your application. To do this, combine the following:  
- [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) stage with `searchBefore` option  
- [`$limit`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/limit/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-limit) stage  
- [toArray()](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.toArray/) and `reverse()` methods.  
For a demonstration of this, see the `searchBefore` query [examples](/docs/search/query/paginate-results#std-label-search-before-egs) on this page.

### `searchBefore` Output  
MongoDB Search returns documents in the results preceding the specified token in reverse order. MongoDB Search also returns the generated tokens for the documents in the results because you specified the `searchSequenceToken` in the [`$project`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/project/#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-project) stage after the [`$search`](/docs/search/query/aggregation-stages/search#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-search) stage (as shown in line 11). These tokens can be used as a reference point for another query with the same semantics.

# Construct a Query Path  
## Overview  
The `path` parameter is used by the MongoDB Search [operators](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/overview#std-label-fts-operators) to specify the field or fields to be searched. It may contain:  
- A string  
- An array of strings  
- A [multi analyzer](/docs/search/index/analyzers/multi#std-label-ref-multi-analyzers) specification  
- An array containing a combination of strings and multi analyzer specifications  
**Note:**  
Not all operators can use all the different types of paths. See the documentation for each individual operator for details on what types of path it supports.

## Usage  
**To search only a single indexed field**, use a quoted string in the `path` parameter. The following example searches a field named `description`.  
```javascript
"path": "description"
```  
**To search multiple indexed fields**, use an array of quoted strings in the `path` parameter. Documents which match on any of the specified fields are included in the result set. The following example searches the `description` and `type` fields.  
```javascript
"path": [ "description", "type" ]
```  
**Note:**  
The `multi` path option is available only to fields of type [string.](/docs/search/index/field-types/string-type#std-label-bson-data-types-string)  
If your [index definition](/docs/search/index/define-field-mappings#std-label-index-config-example) contains a field with multiple analyzers, you can specify which one to use. The `path` parameter can take an object with the following fields:  
| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `value` | The name of the field to search. |
| `multi` | The name of the alternate analyzer specified in a `multi` object in an index definition. To learn more, see [Multi Analyzer.](/docs/search/index/analyzers/multi#std-label-ref-multi-analyzers) |
| `wildcard` | The object containing the wildcard character `*` to match any character in the name of the field to search, including nested fields. A wildcard path: Must be defined as an object.; Cannot contain the `value` or `multi` option.; Cannot contain multiple consecutive wildcard characters such as `**`. Wildcard path is only accepted by the following operators: [phrase](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/phrase#std-label-phrase-ref); [regex](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/regex#std-label-regex-ref); [text](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/text#std-label-text-ref); [wildcard](/docs/search/query/operators-collectors/wildcard#std-label-wildcard-ref) Wildcard path is also accepted for [highlighting.](/docs/search/query/highlighting#std-label-highlight-ref) |  
In the following index definition, fields named `names` and `notes` use the [standard](/docs/search/index/analyzers/standard#std-label-ref-standard-analyzer) analyzer. A field named `comments` uses `standard` as its default analyzer, and it also specifies a `multi` named `mySecondaryAnalyzer` which uses the [lucene.whitespace](/docs/search/index/analyzers/whitespace#std-label-ref-whitespace-analyzer) analyzer.  
```json
{
"mappings": {
"dynamic": false,
"fields": {
"names": {
"type": "string",
"analyzer": "lucene.standard"
},
"notes": {
"type": "string",
"analyzer": "lucene.standard"
},
"comments": {
"type": "string",
"analyzer": "lucene.standard",
"multi": {
"mySecondaryAnalyzer": {
"analyzer": "lucene.whitespace",
"type": "string"
}
}
}
}
}
}
```  
The following `path` example searches the `comments` field using the `multi` named `mySecondaryAnalyzer` in the index definition.  
```javascript
"path": { "value": "comments", "multi": "mySecondaryAnalyzer" }
```  
**To search a combination of indexed fields and fields with multiple
analyzers**, use an array. The following example searches the `names` and `notes` fields with the default analyzer, and the `comments` field using the `multi` named `mySecondaryAnalyzer` in the index definition.  
```javascript
"path": [ "names", "notes", { "value": "comments", "multi": "mySecondaryAnalyzer" } ]
```  
The following `path` example searches all the fields that contain the letter `n` followed by any characters, and the `comments` field using the `multi` named `mySecondaryAnalyzer` in the index definition.  
```javascript
"path": [{ "wildcard": "n*" }, { "value": "comments", "multi": "mySecondaryAnalyzer" }]
```
